analysis.one_liner: Forces dominant hospitals to bill all patients at Medicare rates and funds antitrust enforcement of hospital mergers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees, got no hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill attacked hospital prices from three angles. Hospitals in highly concentrated markets would have had to charge every patient, including the privately insured, the Medicare rate. Hospital-owned clinics away from the main campus would be paid at cheaper doctor-office rates, and hospitals would have to post what they actually charge for their 100 most-used services. It also gave the FTC $160 million to investigate hospital mergers and offered states $1 billion a year in infrastructure grants if they dropped rules that limit competition, like certificate-of-need laws that let regulators block new clinics.
analysis.who_benefits: Privately insured and uninsured patients who get treated at hospitals that dominate their local market, since those patients could no longer be billed hospital rates far above Medicare rates. Taxpayers also benefit from lower federal payments for hospital outpatient clinics and from more antitrust scrutiny of mergers. States that let nurse practitioners and physician assistants practice fully would become eligible for hospital infrastructure grants.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals in urban markets where concentration is very high (a Herfindahl-Hirschman Index above 4,000, or above 5,000 in rural areas) would have to apply Medicare reimbursement rates to all patients, including people with private insurance and people with no insurance, starting in 2021.

Hospitals would have to publicly post the volume-weighted average price they charge for each of the 100 most highly utilized hospital services, in a standardized digital system built by the Secretary of Health and Human Services.

Services in off-campus hospital-owned departments would be paid at the physician-office fee schedule rather than the higher hospital outpatient rate, which lowers Medicare spending and, in concentrated markets, the benchmark prices private patients face.
The FTC would receive $160 million in dedicated funding to hire staff to investigate anticompetitive hospital mergers and practices under the Sherman Antitrust Act.

States would become eligible for $1 billion per year in hospital infrastructure grants through 2028 if they have no certificate-of-need law, allow nurse practitioners and physician assistants to diagnose and treat patients independently, or do not force managed care plans to accept every willing provider.
The bill eliminates shared-savings bonus payments in the Medicare Shared Savings Program, ending payments to provider groups out of Medicare savings.

analysis.who_pays: Hospital systems, especially large consolidated ones in markets where they face little competition, would bear the cost: they would lose private-payer revenue above Medicare rates, lose the higher hospital rates for off-campus clinics, and lose shared-savings bonuses. Provider groups in Medicare accountable care organizations would also lose their shared-savings payments.

drawbacks.text: Applying Medicare rates to all patients at dominant hospitals is an abrupt, unprecedented price ceiling on private payments; hospitals would lose the private-payer revenue that offsets losses on Medicare and Medicaid patients, with no phase-in beyond a 2021 start date and no offsetting funding for hospital operations.

The repeal of shared savings removes the incentive that pays accountable care organizations for keeping Medicare spending down; eliminating it entirely, rather than restructuring it, risks pushing providers out of coordinated-care arrangements altogether.

Site-neutral payment cuts hospital revenue for clinic-based care without distinguishing hospitals that use outpatient margins to cross-subsidize emergency, trauma, and teaching services from those that simply overcharge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients and taxpayers the potential benefit is large: real prices posted publicly, a cap on what monopolized hospitals can charge the privately insured, and lower federal outpatient payments. But the design is blunt. The Medicare-rate mandate hits hospitals all at once in 2021 with no transition aid, and the shared-savings repeal is a full cut rather than a fix. An honest supporter would acknowledge that safety-net hospitals in concentrated markets could be squeezed hard even as their patients gained.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and two subcommittees, and no committee ever held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jim Banks of Indiana introduced the bill on October 23, 2018, the final months of the 115th Congress.

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees, and then to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on October 25, 2018 and the Judiciary antitrust subcommittee on November 15, 2018.
No hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill attracted only one cosponsor, so it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consolidated hospital systems and provider groups are better off because the bill died: they continue charging private insurers and patients hospital-set rates above Medicare rates, billing hospital rates for off-campus clinics, and keeping shared-savings payments, with no public price-posting requirement and no added antitrust enforcement of hospital mergers.

for.name: Rep. Jim Banks
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

against.name: Rep. Greg Walden
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill's health provisions stayed in subcommittee after referral.

against.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill's Medicare payment provisions.

against.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill's antitrust provisions; the antitrust subcommittee referral produced no action.

against.name: Speaker Paul Ryan
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; the multi-committee referral it received left it without a scheduled path to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's entire sponsorship was two Republicans, and no committee or floor action ever occurred.

industries.industry: Consolidated hospital systems in concentrated markets
industries.note: These hospitals would have had to bill every patient, including the privately insured and uninsured, at Medicare rates, ending the private-payer revenue above Medicare that supports much of their margin. For patients in markets dominated by one or two hospital systems, that revenue comes from prices with little competitive check on them.

industries.industry: Hospital operators of off-campus provider-based departments
industries.note: Site-neutral payment would have ended their ability to bill higher hospital outpatient rates for freestanding clinics, a practice that costs patients and Medicare more than the same care in a doctor's office.

industries.industry: Medicare accountable care organization provider groups
industries.note: The bill repeals shared-savings payments entirely. Those payments came out of Medicare savings, so ending them keeps the savings with taxpayers, but it also removes the incentive structure meant to keep providers in coordinated-care arrangements.

industries.industry: Nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and other advanced practice clinicians
industries.note: States that let these clinicians diagnose and treat patients independently would qualify for $1 billion annual infrastructure grants, expanding patient access to lower-cost care.
